Most notably, show record beating performance on the ImageNet 2012 classification benchmark, with their convnet model achieving an error rate of 16.4%, compared to the 2nd place result of 26.1%.
The model was trained on the ImageNet 2012 training set (1.3 million images, spread over 1000 different classes).
Dropout is used in the fully connected layers (6 and 7) with a rate of 0.5.
This dataset consists of 1.3M/50k/100k training/validation/test examples, spread over 1000 categories. ImageNet shows our results on this dataset.
The pre-trained model beats the best reported result for 30 images/class from by 2.2%.
The convnet model trained from scratch however does terribly, only achieving 46.5%.
Our ImageNet-pretrained model beats the current state-of-the-art results obtained by Bo by a significant margin: 74.2% vs 55.2% for 60 training images/class.

One difference is that the sparse connections used in Krizhevsky's layers 3,4,5 (due to the model being split across 2 GPUs) are replaced with dense connections in our model.

tables.caption: Measure of correspondence for different object parts in 5 different dog images. The lower scores for the eyes and nose (compared to random object parts) show the model implicitly establishing some form of correspondence of parts at layer 5 in the model. At layer 7, the scores are more similar, perhaps due to upper layers trying to discriminate between the different breeds of dog.
